subject: Engelska 7
title: Grammar: advanced tenses and modality
sourceSummary: Nuanced modal verbs (must/have to/should/ought to/might have), future perfect and future continuous, and the subjunctive in formal English.
topics: modal verbs of deduction and obligation

questions.topic: modal verbs of deduction and obligation
questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses a logical deduction rather than an obligation?
questions.opener: Think about the difference between "must" as a rule and "must" as a deduction.
choices: You must complete the form before Friday.
You have to wear a helmet on a construction site.
He must have left already — his coat is gone.
Students must attend at least 80% of lessons.
questions.explanation: "He must have left already" is a logical deduction based on evidence (the coat is gone), not a rule. The other options express obligation or requirement.

questions.topic: modal verbs of deduction and obligation
questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that expresses a strong recommendation rather than a strict obligation.
questions.opener: "Ought to" is stronger than "could" but weaker than "must" — it's advice, not a requirement.
choices: You must renew your driving licence before it expires.
You really ought to see a doctor about that cough.
You have to submit your tax return by the deadline.
Passengers must fasten their seatbelts.
questions.explanation: "Ought to" gives strong advice without it being legally or formally binding. The other sentences describe rules or legal requirements where "must"/"have to" is correct.

questions.topic: modal verbs of deduction and obligation
questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with the modal verb that best fits: 'The museum is closed and the lights are off. They ___ already gone home.'
questions.opener: The evidence (closed, dark) points to a confident conclusion, not a guess.
choices: might have
should have
can't have
must have
questions.explanation: "Must have" expresses a strong, evidence-based conclusion. "Might have" would have fitted if it were just a possibility, and "can't have" is used to rule something out — the opposite of what the evidence shows here.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: 'By the time the plane lands, we ___ for over ten hours.'
questions.opener: An ongoing action that has continued up to a future point in time — which form signals that?
choices: will travel
will have been travelling
travel
will be travelling
questions.explanation: The future perfect continuous ("will have been travelling") is used for actions that have continued over a period up to a specified future point in time. "Will be travelling" (future continuous) simply describes an action in progress at that point, without emphasising duration.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the future continuous to describe an action in progress at a specific future moment?
questions.opener: Which form describes something in progress at a specific future point in time?
choices: This time next week, I will be lying on a beach in Greece.
This time next week, I will have lain on a beach in Greece.
This time next week, I lie on a beach in Greece.
This time next week, I will lain on a beach in Greece.
questions.explanation: "Will be lying" (future continuous) describes an action in progress at a specified future point in time. "Will have lain" (future perfect) would instead mean that the action was already completed by that point.

questions.prompt: Choose the grammatically correct, formal sentence.
questions.opener: In formal, hypothetical English, a special verb form is used after "if", regardless of the subject.
choices: If I was you, I would accept the offer.
If I would be you, I would accept the offer.
If I were you, I would accept the offer.
If I am you, I would accept the offer.
questions.explanation: In hypothetical if-clauses, the subjunctive form "were" is used for all persons, even "I" and "he/she": "If I were you...". "Was" is common in spoken English but is not considered correct in formal English.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence in correct, formal English and explain the grammar: 'It is essential that he attends the interview on time.'
questions.opener: After expressions like "it is essential/important/vital that", a special verb form is used — the base form, regardless of subject.
questions.answer: It is essential that he attend the interview on time.
steps: This is called the mandative subjunctive and is used after expressions like "it is essential/important/vital/necessary that".
The verb after "that" takes its base form (bare infinitive without "to"), regardless of subject — so "attend", not "attends".
This applies even in the third person singular, unlike ordinary present tense where we normally add -s.
In more everyday American and British English, "should attend" is sometimes heard instead, but in formal written English (reports, memos) the subjunctive form is preferred.

questions.topic: modal verbs of deduction and obligation
questions.prompt: Summarise the key differences between must, have to, should, ought to, and the modal perfect forms (must have / might have / can't have).
questions.opener: A quick overview of the most nuanced modal verbs.
questions.answer: must = strong obligation (the speaker's own rule) or a strong deduction · have to = obligation imposed from outside (law, rule, circumstance) · should/ought to = recommendation, not requirement; "ought to" is slightly more formal · must have + past participle = confident conclusion about the past · might/could have = possible conclusion · can't have = ruled-out conclusion (the opposite of must have) · should have = an expectation that was not met, often with regret

questions.topic: modal verbs of deduction and obligation
questions.prompt: Choose the modal that best fits: 'She ___ be at work now — I just saw her car in the driveway.'
questions.opener: The evidence (the car is in the driveway) rules out a possibility — which modal verb expresses that?
choices: can't
must
should
has to
questions.explanation: "Can't" expresses a ruled-out conclusion based on evidence, the opposite of "must". The other options express obligation or a positive conclusion, which doesn't fit the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the subjunctive correctly after a suggestion verb?
questions.opener: "Suggest that" belongs to the same family of verbs requiring the subjunctive as "recommend that".
choices: I suggest that she see a specialist as soon as possible.
I suggest that she sees a specialist as soon as possible.
I suggest that she will see a specialist as soon as possible.
I suggest that she saw a specialist as soon as possible.
questions.explanation: Verbs like "suggest", "recommend", "insist", and "demand" are followed by the subjunctive form (base form) in the that-clause: "that she see", not "sees"/"will see"/"saw".

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: 'Don't call at 8pm — I ___ dinner then.'
questions.opener: An action in progress AT a specific future point in time.
choices: will be having
will have had
have
will having
questions.explanation: The future continuous ("will be having") describes an action in progress at 8pm that evening. "Will have had" (future perfect) would have meant dinner was already finished.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: 'By next June, she ___ at the company for exactly five years.'
questions.opener: An action that is completed/has reached a certain duration BY a future point in time.
choices: will have worked
will work
will be working
works
questions.explanation: The future perfect ("will have worked") is used to express that something will have been achieved or completed by a specific future point in time — here that the five-year mark is reached in June.

questions.prompt: Choose the correctly formed sentence using the mandative subjunctive.
questions.opener: After "recommended that", the same subjunctive form (base form) is used as after "essential that".
choices: The committee recommended that the policy be reviewed annually.
The committee recommended that the policy is reviewed annually.
The committee recommended that the policy was reviewed annually.
The committee recommended that the policy will be reviewed annually.
questions.explanation: The verb after "recommended that" takes the bare-infinitive form (subjunctive): "be reviewed", regardless of subject or tense in the main clause. The other forms ("is", "was", "will be") are all incorrect in this construction.

questions.topic: modal verbs of deduction and obligation
questions.prompt: Which sentence best expresses a strong prohibition rather than mere advice?
questions.opener: "Must not" is stronger and more absolute than "shouldn't".
choices: You must not disclose confidential information to third parties.
You shouldn't share confidential information carelessly.
You might not want to share that.
It's probably best not to mention it.
questions.explanation: "Must not" expresses a strict prohibition, often with legal or regulatory weight, while the other options merely give advice or soft recommendations.

questions.prompt: 'At 3pm tomorrow, the technicians ___ the server for two hours already.' Choose the correct form.
questions.opener: The emphasis is on HOW LONG the action has already been going on at the future point in time.
choices: will have been repairing
will be repairing
will repair
repair
questions.explanation: The future perfect continuous ("will have been repairing") emphasizes the duration of an action that has already continued up to a specific future point in time (3pm, for two hours). "Will be repairing" (future continuous) would only describe an ongoing action without specifying duration.
